title: Why Elevator “Wizards” Are Hard to Find – and What It Means for You
excerpt: Even with good pay, the U.S. faces a growing shortage of elevator mechanics, a problem highlighted by veteran technician Jim Lembesis.
body:
When a lift stalls in a Chicago high‑rise, building managers often call on a seasoned technician named Jim Lembesis. After nearly five decades on the job, Lembesis knows the anxiety that residents feel when they’re stuck – especially seniors and wheelchair users who rely on elevators daily. “They wait and they wait,” he says, describing the frustration that builds when a lift repeatedly fails.

## The Growing Shortage of Lift Technicians

The shortage of elevator and escalator mechanics has been a headline in the BBC’s recent coverage. While the average U.S. salary for a lift mechanic sits around $110,000 (£83,000), the trade is still struggling to attract newcomers. One hurdle is the four‑year apprenticeship required to become certified, a program overseen by the National Association for Elevator Contractors. Many states also demand licensing, adding another layer of complexity. As Matt Hollinshead, the association’s president, explains, the combination of lengthy training and stringent regulations makes it harder to fill open positions.

## Why the Job Is Both Tough and Rewarding

Working on lifts isn’t without danger. Technicians face risks of falls, electrocution, and even odd mishaps – Lembesis recalls being struck on the head by an umbrella after rescuing a passenger. Yet the camaraderie among mechanics and the “wizard‑like” skill set keep many in the trade. They often carry spare door parts in their vans because, according to Lembesis, doors are the most trouble‑prone component, taking constant abuse from carts and debris.

## Parts Shortages and Aging Equipment

Delays in repairs aren’t always about staffing. Some setbacks stem from the time it takes to manufacture replacement parts, such as hydraulic cylinders that can require six to twelve weeks to produce. Older elevators, many over a century old, demand specialized knowledge that only seasoned technicians possess. When parts aren’t readily available, building managers may wait days just to get a diagnosis, compounding residents’ inconvenience.

## Looking Ahead

Industry voices suggest that early exposure to the trade in high schools and technical colleges could spark interest among younger workers. Recruiter Matt Allred, host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasizes the blend of mechanical know‑how and problem‑solving that makes the role unique. Meanwhile, some large manufacturers have been criticized for tightening maintenance contracts, limiting third‑party repairs and further straining the already thin pool of technicians.

The shortage of these modern‑day “wizards” highlights a hidden but essential part of urban life. As cities grow taller and reliance on vertical transport increases, ensuring a steady pipeline of skilled lift mechanics will be crucial to keeping everyone moving safely and efficiently.
